source_read: Publisher HTML (link.springer.com, Harm Reduction Journal 15, article 46, 2018; open access), reached through https://doi.org/10.1186/s12954-018-0252-8 in my own browser tab: the article page read in full (abstract, Background, Methods with Setting, Data collection, Data analysis and Ethics, Results, Discussion, Conclusions, abbreviations, reference list, funding, data availability, author information and contributions, ethics, competing interests); Table 1 and Table 2 read as text with their footnotes on their own pages (.../tables/1 and .../tables/2); Fig. 1 is a photograph of a strip (legend only). Editors' calculations recomputed with Wilson and Newcombe intervals and Woolf odds-ratio intervals.

claims.overstatement: Slight, in the lead sentence only: it says a positive result was followed, by people's own account, by a safer way of using. At Vancouver what was recorded was an intention stated to staff at the time of a check made before use, not an account of what people later did. The Vancouver sentence itself is worded correctly (staff recorded an intention; what people then did was not recorded). Suggest 'by people's own account or stated intention' in the lead sentence.
claims.note: Recomputed from Table 1 (pre-consumption checks only): intended dose reduction 142/391 = 36.3% (Wilson 31.7-41.2%) after a positive result against 7/122 = 5.7% (2.8-11.4%) after a negative one; crude OR from the counts 9.37 (Woolf 4.25-20.65), printed 9.36 (4.25-20.65); risk difference 30.6 points (Newcombe 23.3-36.3); intended disposal 50/436 = 11.5% against 10/134 = 7.5%, OR 1.61 (0.79-3.26), printed 1.60. All match the claim and its magnitude. The unit is checks by anonymous clients (number of people unknown), which the claim respects; the abstract and Results call them participants. The abstract and text print 11.4% for the 11.47% in Table 1.

anchors.locator: Table 1, dose-reduction panel (footnote a: pre-consumption checks only)
anchors.extracted: Positive pre-consumption checks 391: intended dose reduction 142 (36.32%), no 249; negative 122: 7 (5.74%), no 115; crude OR 9.36 (95% CI 4.25-20.65), P = 0.0001 (chi-square or Fisher's exact test).
Positive pre-consumption checks 436: intended disposal 50 (11.47%), no 386; negative 134: 10 (7.46%), no 124; OR 1.60 (0.79-3.26), P = 0.186.

After a positive pre-consumption check 36.3% (n = 142) planned to reduce the dose and 11.4% (n = 50) to dispose of the drug; dose-reduction OR 9.36 (4.25-20.65); disposal OR 1.60 (0.79-3.26), not significant. Described as participants although the unit is checks.

After the result clients were asked whether they planned to reduce the dose or dispose of the drug; staff recorded yes/no intentions on the reporting form with result, timing, client-reported substance, overdose after consumption (judged by nursing staff) and naloxone; the amount actually used and any disposal were not recorded; data anonymous, Insite IDs not linked.
Limitations: anonymous data, so results cannot be interpreted per client; how many individual clients used the service, and whether they used it repeatedly, is unknown.

claims.note: The source bears on three parts of the claim. (1) It has no comparison of people given strips with people not given them, consistent with the claim. (2) 'No study read reports what people did after a negative result' holds for behaviour, but this study reports intentions and an observed outcome after negative results: after 122 negative pre-consumption checks 7 (5.7%) intended to use less and after 134, 10 (7.5%) intended disposal; none of 107 negative pre-consumption checks was followed by an overdose (Wilson 0-3.5%, editors' calculation), against 7 of 357 positive ones (2.0%). These staff-observed data, small and from a supervised site where nurses respond, are the only outcome data after a negative result among my three sources; the claim could mention them. (3) The authors relay the criticism that drug checking can create an unjustified feeling of safety, told every client with a negative result that it could not exclude other potent adulterants, and raise, without data, that some clients might seek fentanyl because overdoses are treated on site.

anchors.extracted: Drug checking has been criticized for creating an unjustified feeling of safety, since the absence of unexpected or potent components in a sample cannot guarantee its safety (refs. 18, 20).

Clients with a negative result were told that the strip tests only for fentanyl and cannot ensure the drug is free of other, possibly more potent adulterants (e.g. W-18); all were offered harm-reduction information, take-home naloxone and training, information on other sites and treatment referral.
After negative pre-consumption checks: intended dose reduction 7 of 122 (5.74%); intended disposal 10 of 134 (7.46%). Intentions only.

Overdose after a positive pre-consumption check 7 of 357 (1.96%) against 0 of 107 after a negative one, OR 4.60 (0.26-81.21, 0.5 added to all cells); naloxone 3 of 355 against 0 of 109 (row printed with 92 no), OR 1.83 (0.09-35.87).
The authors raise the possibility, to be explored in future studies, that some clients sought out fentanyl knowing an overdose can be treated at the supervised site.

Concerns (including a Health Canada advisory) that strips may miss novel fentanyl analogues and give a small number of false negatives; the authors advise distributing information on the tests' limitations and continued use of other harm-reduction practices.

claims.overstatement: Two slight points. (1) 'Among people who use opioids, few said they got rid of a drug after a strip showed fentanyl': at Vancouver people stated before use that they intended to dispose of the drug; nobody reported having disposed of it (the next clause, staff recorded an intention, is correct). Suggest 'few said they would get rid of, or had got rid of, a drug'. (2) The checks were of client-reported substances, mostly but not only heroin, so 'people who use opioids' is approximate. The authors' reasons for the low rate (dependence, no money for replacement drugs, no access to unadulterated drugs) are their suggestion without data; 'suggest' would be more exact than 'link'.
claims.note: Recomputed: 50/436 = 11.47% (Wilson 8.8-14.8%), 10/134 = 7.46% (4.1-13.2%); OR from the counts 1.61 (0.79-3.26), printed 1.60; risk difference 4.0 points (Newcombe -2.3 to 8.7), as in the magnitude. The abstract and Results print 11.4% for 11.47%. The Discussion relays, from a 2015 festival report (ref. 23, Sage 2016, the same report that Maghsoudi et al. 2022 cite for 4% observed disposal), 13% disposal after an unexpected result against 2% after an expected one.

anchors.extracted: Pre-consumption checks: intended disposal after 50 of 436 positive (11.47%) against 10 of 134 negative (7.46%); OR 1.60 (0.79-3.26), P = 0.186.
Only 11.4% (n = 50) planned disposal after a positive pre-consumption check; odds higher after a positive result but not significantly (OR 1.60, 0.79-3.26).

Results encouraged plans to reduce the dose but most clients did not plan disposal, unlike a 2015 festival service where 13% disposed after unexpected and 2% after expected results (ref. 23); the authors suggest Insite clients may be dependent, lack funds for replacement drugs and lack access to unadulterated drugs.
Disposal recorded by staff as a stated intention (yes/no) with the client-reported substance (e.g. heroin, methamphetamine or cocaine); not followed up.
The majority of checks were of client-reported heroin, 84.1% (n = 939) of them positive; other substances were also checked.

claims.overstatement: One misstatement of sequence: '113 of the 120 overdoses recorded followed checks made after use'. The source says the 113 overdoses were reported among clients who tested after consumption; the order of overdose and check was not captured, and the authors say a check after use may have been prompted by an overdose. Replace 'followed' with 'were recorded with' (as the magnitude already says). Also, 'neither with a comparison group' (relayed from the scoping review) fits this study only in the sense of no group that did not test: it compares positive with negative checks, and checks with and without an intention to use less.
claims.note: Supported: most checks after use (58%, n = 789; 789/1411 = 55.9%, so about 1360 checks had timing recorded); 113 of 120 overdoses among post-consumption checks (Table 2: 108 + 5 after use, 7 + 0 before use); crude OR 0.41 (0.18-0.89) for intended dose reduction among all participants, i.e. pooled across timing. Editors' check of the pooling: 7 overdoses printed as 4.5% imply about 156 checks with an intention to use less, 149 of them pre-consumption (Table 1); overdose was recorded with 7 of 464 pre-consumption checks (1.5%) against 113 of 778 post-consumption checks (14.5%), so the timing of the check alone can produce the low odds ratio (a rough reconstruction from these totals gives OR 0.42, 0.19-0.91). The authors caution against reading the overdose associations, yet also write that drug checking at a supervised site might let clients lower their overdose risk and conclude that it could contribute to preventing overdoses.

anchors.extracted: The majority of checks were performed post-consumption (58%; n = 789); post-consumption checks were more often positive (82.9%, n = 654) than pre-consumption checks (76.5%, n = 438).

120 overdoses recorded in association with checks, 94% (n = 113) among those who tested post-consumption; among all participants, intended dose reduction associated with lower odds of overdose, OR 0.41 (0.18-0.89), and of naloxone, OR 0.38 (0.15-0.96); 4.5% (n = 7) of those intending to reduce overdosed. These two ORs are in the text only, with no table.

Overdose after positive against negative checks: pre-consumption 7/357 (1.96%) against 0/107, OR 4.60 (0.26-81.21, 0.5 added); post-consumption 108/649 (16.64%) against 5/129 (3.88%), OR 4.95 (1.97-12.39); overall 115/1028 against 5/242, OR 5.97 (2.41-14.78).

Caution: most checks were post-consumption; the timeline and sequence of the decision to check were not captured; a check after use may have been prompted by an overdose. The authors still say drug checking at a supervised site might help clients reduce overdose risk, adding that further research is needed.
Drug checking at harm-reduction facilities might be feasible and could contribute to preventing overdoses: an interpretation stronger than the crude, timing-confounded data.

claims.note: Recomputed: 1411/134,176 = 1.05% (Wilson 1.0-1.1%). The period 7 July 2016 to 21 June 2017 is 350 days inclusive, giving 383 visits a day from the total, below the printed minimum of 387; at the printed average of 533 a day the total would be about 186,550 and the share 0.76%; 1411 checks over 350 days give 4.03 a day, matching the printed 4.0. So 'about 1 in 100 visits' (about 1% or less) is right. The Discussion compares uptake with a festival (3224 checks among more than 67,000 attendees) and with stated willingness (43% in London, Ontario; over 90% of 93 young adults in Rhode Island, which it attributes to ref. 11, Kenney et al. 2018, a citation slip: the Rhode Island study is Krieger et al. 2018).

anchors.extracted: Clients learned of the service from posters; staff offered all clients the chance to check their drugs for fentanyl as they entered the injection room; checking before or after use was the client's choice.
7 July 2016 to 21 June 2017: 134,176 visits, an average of 533 a day (range 387-780); 1411 visits (1%) led to a check by clients, 4.0 checks a day (range 0-27).
How many individual clients used the service, and whether they kept using it, is unknown (anonymous data).

Uptake described as low (1% of visits); compared with a festival service and with stated willingness in London, Ontario (43%) and Rhode Island (over 90%); low uptake may reflect clients assuming most street drugs are adulterated; results posted on site may have informed clients who did not check.

claims.note: This study recorded nothing about the people who checked, so it gives no data on who tests. It supports the claim's self-selection point only through the authors' suggestion that the service, used in about 1% of visits, may have attracted clients more likely to use harm-reduction strategies, and that the data may over-represent clients more likely to have fentanyl in their drugs.

anchors.extracted: As only a small proportion of Insite clients used the service, it may have attracted clients more likely to engage in harm-reduction strategies (authors' suggestion, no data).
The data may come from clients more likely to have fentanyl in their drugs; limited generalizability.
No demographic or identifying information was collected and Insite IDs were not linked, so checkers cannot be compared with non-checkers.

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed: 350 days inclusive; 134,176/350 = 383 a day; 134,176/533 = 252 days; 1411/4.0 = 353 days.
Recomputed with 0.5 added: 1.84 (0.09-35.88) with 92 checks without naloxone, 2.17 (0.11-42.42) with 109.
The aim of positivity by substance type is stated in Background, 5th paragraph; only heroin is reported.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I with critical overall is right for any effect of checking or of intending to use less; all printed Table 2 odds ratios re-derive from the counts (5.97, 4.60, 4.95, 4.42, 3.68 within rounding), and the timing confounding described in the confounding note is borne out by the editors' reconstruction of the OR 0.41 (about 0.42 from timing alone).

missed: Discussion, 4th paragraph: the willingness of 93 young adults in Rhode Island is attributed to ref. 11, which is Kenney et al. 2018 (people in opioid withdrawal management); the Rhode Island study is Krieger et al. 2018. A citation slip; cite Krieger directly for that figure.

Abstract › Results and Results, 2nd paragraph call the 142 and 50 'participants'; they are checks by anonymous clients (the card's design_detail says units are checks; this could be listed as a minor reporting issue).
